title: Errors, importing, and exporting
jupyter: python3
---

A Starsim model is written as Python, and that code is the model: it is what is kept, shared, and compared (with a diff in a text editor, or by the results it gives). This page covers the messages Starsim gives when something is wrong, the importers and exporters, and how the size of the language is kept in check.

## Ways to write a model out

| What | Method | Holds | Read back? |
|---|---|---|---|
| The code | the script itself; for an import, `sim.imported.code` | the model, as Python | yes, by running it |
| Results as JSON | `sim.to_json()` | parameters, summary, and results, for use elsewhere | no |
| A saved sim | `ss.save('run.sim', sim)` | the sim itself (a pickle), including partway through a run | yes, with `ss.load()` |
| Another framework's format | `ss.export_to(sim, 'odin')` | the compartmental form of the declared diseases | yes, with `ss.import_from()` |

## Errors, warnings, and notes

The policy is: **prefer guessing a default and printing it to raising an error.** An error is for when there is no sensible guess: a name that doesn't exist, lengths that don't match, a request the solver can't meet. Every message is meant to be read once, by an epidemiologist or by an AI writing a model for one, so it uses the user's own names, says what exists instead, and says what to do:

```{python}
import starsim as ss
ss.options(jupyter=True)

S, I, R = ss.states('S I R')
sir = ss.Disease(infection=S >> I @ 0.05 * I, recovery=I >> R @ ss.days(7), init_prev=0.01, name='sir')
sim = ss.Sim(sir, pars=dict(betta=0.2), verbose=0)
try:
    sim.init()
except KeyError as e:
    print(f'{type(e).__name__}: {e}')
```

There are three levels:

| Level | Type | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| Error | a built-in exception: a `KeyError` for a name that is not found, a `TypeError` for a value of the wrong kind, a `ValueError` for the rest | raises; caught by type, e.g. `except KeyError` |
| Warning | a `RuntimeWarning` | issued through Python's warnings, so filters (and `ss.options.warnings='error'`) apply; the run continues |
| Note | `ss.note()` | kept in `sim.notes` whatever the verbosity, and printed as one line when `verbose` is 1 or more |

Five errors and four warnings are classes of their own in `ss.errors`, since code catches or filters them by kind: `ss.CapabilityError` (the solver asked for can't run part of the model, which `solver='auto'` catches to run as agents), `ss.AlreadyRunError`, the distribution errors `DistNotInitializedError` and `DistSeedRepeatError`, and `BooleanOperationError`; and the warnings `AtBound`, `NotConverged`, `LossyExport`, and `ImportIncomplete`. The tests check each error, warning, and note by its message (`tests/devtests/test_errors.py`).

## Importers and exporters

Every importer reads another framework's model into one intermediate object, `ss.io.Source` (its states, parameters, flows as rate expressions, stratifications, outcomes, and what it couldn't translate). One function, `ss.io.write()`, writes a `Source` as Starsim code (a declared `ss.Disease`, with its parameters, states, and transitions as variables, ending with `sim = ss.Sim(...)`), by the same rules for every format, and `ss.io.build()` runs that code to make the sim. So there is one path, from a foreign model to code to a sim, and never from a sim back to code; each framework needs only a reader, and there are no framework-to-framework converters. The code is kept as `sim.imported.code`, for the user to keep and change. A value the writer can't write as code, such as a network, is given by the importer as `ss.io.Code('...')`, the Python that makes it.

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
flowchart LR
  F["odin, SBML, EMULSION, SimInf,<br>flepiMoP, summer2, Atomica, camdl,<br>EpiModel, epydemix, MEmilio"] --> R[reader] --> S["ss.io.Source"] --> W["ss.io.write()"] --> C["Starsim code"] --> Sim[sim]
  Sim --> E["SBML, odin"]
```

The hardest part of importing is reading rates. Most frameworks write a flow as a total, such as `beta * S * I / N`; the importer turns it into a per-person rate on a transition, and says how it read each one. A rate divided by the population total is exposure through the routes (`beta * I`); one without the division is density-dependent and is kept as a count (`beta * I.n`); anything else is kept literally, as an expression of counts, which is exact under every solver. A `Source` can also be filled in by hand:

```{python}

src = ss.io.Source('sir', format='by hand')
for name, n in dict(S=990, I=10, R=0).items():
    src.add_state(name, init=n)
src.add_par('beta', 0.3)
src.add_par('gamma', 0.1)
src.add_flow('S', 'I', rate='beta * S * I / (S + I + R)', per='total', name='infection')
src.add_flow('I', 'R', rate='gamma * I', per='total', name='recovery')
sim = ss.io.build(src, stop=100)
print(sim.imported.code)
print(ss.export_to(sim, 'odin'))
```

An importer keeps the source's names, marks what it guessed (as `[guessed]` in `describe()`, like a hand-written model), keeps going when something doesn't map onto a built-in piece, and lists what it couldn't translate by name (`ss.errors.ImportIncomplete`, also in `sim.imported.incomplete`). An incomplete import still runs, without the listed parts, and the warning says how to finish it with the `import-model` skill. Exporters work the other way: SBML and odin are written from the built model (each disease's graph and engine, in its compartmental form), and each export lists what it left out or changed (`LossyExport`), one line per declaration. `ss.io.to_hub()` writes the runs of a MultiSim as a forecast-hub submission.

Each importer is tested against its framework's own examples (`tests/devtests/io/`) and in a scaled-down demo per framework (`tests/switching/`). The [Coming from](../coming_from/index.qmd) pages show the translations side by side.

## The vocabulary

A language nobody can hold in their head is one nobody uses correctly, so the design record lists every public name in one place.

The capitalization rule is Starsim's existing one: modules, containers, and base classes are CamelCase (`ss.Sim`, `ss.Disease`, `ss.Vaccine`); the pieces you put inside them are lowercase (`ss.days`, `ss.normal`, `ss.modify`, `ss.vaccinate`). Before a name is added: does Starsim already have one; can it be written with what exists (a bednet is an `ss.modify`, a metapopulation a stratification by patch); would more than one kind of model use it; is a keyword enough?

The code is in `starsim/internals/errors.py` and `starsim/io/` (`core.py` holds `Source`, `write()`, and `build()`, with one file per framework, and `export.py` the exporters).

## Limits

- A sim made in Starsim is not written back out as Starsim code: its code is the script that made it. Only an import is written as code.
- Exports to other formats carry less than the code does: a network, a module written as code, and a function are listed as left out.
